body.text: After this chapter, other people's list code reads smoothly and yours gets shorter.

slides.title: sort and sorted
slides.sub: In place or a new list
slides.main: sorted breaks nothing: the original order stays intact.

body.text:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
print(sorted(nums))        # [1, 2, 3]
print(nums)                # [3, 1, 2] — untouched
nums.sort(reverse=True)    # in place, descending
print(nums)                # [3, 2, 1]

cells.title: nums = nums.sort()
cells.sub: Mistake: the name ends up None

slides.title: Strings and case
slides.sub: Capitals first; digit strings sort as text
slides.main: Normalize case before comparing, convert strings to numbers.

body.text:
words = ["watermelon", "Apple", "banana"]
print(sorted(words))
print(sorted(["10", "2", "1"]))
ON SCREEN

['Apple', 'banana', 'watermelon']
['1', '10', '2']
Python refuses to sort numbers and strings together — an error.

slides.title: The key parameter
slides.sub: Sort by a value computed from each item
slides.main: Pass the function without parentheses: you hand it over, not call it.

body.text:
words = ["ccc", "a", "bb"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))
names = ["vera", "Anya", "boris"]
print(sorted(names, key=str.lower))
ON SCREEN

['a', 'bb', 'ccc']
['Anya', 'boris', 'vera']
The sort is stable: equal keys keep their original order.

slides.title: Order tricks
slides.main: Small bricks — sorted, a slice, equality — build solutions.

body.text:
nums = [5, 1, 9, 3]
print(sorted(nums, reverse=True)[:3])   # [9, 5, 3]
for x in reversed(nums):                # from the end: 3, 9, 1, 5
    print(x)
print(nums == sorted(nums))             # False
Sorting costs time: not for one maximum — there is max.

slides.title: List comprehension
slides.sub: A loop with append — in one line
slides.main: Reads like a phrase: "the square of x for each x in these numbers".

slides.title: A condition in a comprehension
slides.sub: if goes last, after the loop header
slides.main: The condition at the end filters, the expression at the start transforms.

body.text:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
evens = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]       # [2, 4, 6]
sq = [x * x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]      # [4, 16, 36]

slides.title: Strings: split and join
slides.main: join takes only strings — convert numbers with str first.

body.text:
words = "hello world".split()
print([len(w) for w in words])         # [5, 5]
print([w.upper() for w in words])      # ['HELLO', 'WORLD']
print(", ".join(words))                # hello, world
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print("+".join([str(n) for n in nums]))   # 1+2+3

slides.title: When a loop is better
slides.main: Good code is not the shortest but the clearest.

slides.title: any and all
slides.sub: Is there at least one — and do all fit
slides.main: These are the quantifiers of discrete math: "exists" and "for all".

body.text:
nums = [5, 120, 8]
print(any(x > 100 for x in nums))    # True
print(all(x > 0 for x in nums))      # True
print(any([]), all([]))              # False True
Empty input: no matches — any gives False; no violators — all gives True.

slides.title: A list as a stack
slides.sub: append pushes on top, pop takes from the top
slides.main: A stack underlies bracket checks, the back button and undo.

body.text:
stack = []
stack.append("(")
stack.append("(")
stack.pop()
print(stack)    # ['(']
